summary: Published for the historical record, this is the Simple Internet Protocol, which was a candidate for the IETF's IPng work that became IPv6. The original draft dated from November 1992 and appears substantially unchanged. It is historic and unrelated to the Session Initiation Protocol.

eli5.summary: Before today's new internet addresses, people proposed several designs. This is one that was not chosen, kept for history.

questions: what is the simple internet protocol sipp
how did sip lead to ipv6
is sip the same as session initiation protocol
subtitle: A 1992 design for a simpler IP with 64-bit addresses, kept for the record as one of the candidates that led to IPv6.

tldr.problem: IP version 4 had 32-bit addresses, and its designers wanted a next-generation IP with room for more levels of address hierarchy while staying simple and fast to implement.
tldr.mechanism: SIP keeps the IPv4 model but widens addresses to 64 bits, uses a fixed-length header without the inessential fields, and moves optional data such as source routing and fragmentation into separate headers.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8507 is Historic. It publishes an incomplete 1992 draft for the record. SIP evolved into SIP Plus, which led eventually to IPv6.

today: RFC 8507 has Historic status and is published only for the historical record, with no statement about value for implementation or deployment. The current IPv6 specification is RFC 8200.

sections.title: What SIP Was Trying to Do
sections.content:
The Simple Internet Protocol (SIP) is a new version of IP. This is not the Session Initiation Protocol that shares the abbreviation. Its main differences from IP version 4 (RFC 791) are three: addresses expand to 64 bits, the header drops some inessential fields, and length restrictions on optional data such as source-routing information are relaxed.

SIP keeps the IP model of globally unique, hierarchically structured addresses. Going from 32 to 64 bits allows more levels of hierarchy, which the text says is enough for tens of thousands of addressable devices in every office, every residence and every vehicle in the world. Fixed-length, compact addresses are meant to keep routers and hosts fast and keep header overhead almost as low as IPv4.

The design stays very close to IPv4 on purpose. That makes it easy to understand, lets implementers reuse code and data structures (including almost all of ICMP and IGMP), and makes translation between SIP and IPv4 packets straightforward.
sections.eli5: SIP is like giving every house a longer street address so the postal system never runs out, while keeping the envelope almost the same as before.

sections.title: The SIP Header
sections.content:
The SIP header is a fixed layout of a 4-bit Version (decimal 6, marked in the text as to be confirmed), a 28-bit Reserved field, a 16-bit Payload Length, an 8-bit Payload Type, an 8-bit Hop Limit, and a 64-bit Source Address and Destination Address.

Payload Length counts everything after the SIP header, in octets. Payload Type says what follows, for example TCP. Hop Limit is decremented by 1 by each system that forwards the packet, and the packet is discarded if it reaches zero. The Reserved field is set to zero when sending and ignored on reception.

Compared with IPv4, the header has no header length (it is fixed), no precedence or type of service, and no header checksum. Appendix A explains that the transport pseudo-header checksum protects destinations from accepting corrupted packets instead.
sections.eli5: The header is the label on the envelope. It says who sent it, who gets it, how big it is, and how many hops it may take before it is thrown away.

sections.title: SIP Addresses
sections.content:
A SIP address is 64 bits (8 octets). In text it is 16 hexadecimal digits with a colon between the 4th and 5th digits, such as 0123:4567:89AB:CDEF. Because at least one colon is always present, SIP addresses are easy to tell apart from domain names and IPv4 addresses.

A unicast address identifies one interface. A system sees it as a subnet prefix of n bits plus an interface ID of 64-n bits, and learns the length from a subnet mask that it gets in the same way as the address. Hosts know nothing about structure beyond that. Routers may learn extra masks, such as a site mask, to see higher levels of the hierarchy. There is no wired-in knowledge of unicast address formats.

A multicast address names a group of interfaces. Its layout is a 1-bit IPv4 compatibility flag, 7 bits of 1111111, 4 flag bits, a 4-bit scope and a 48-bit group ID. The scope values include intra-system (1), intra-link (2), intra-site (5), intra-metro (8), intra-country (B) and global (E).

Special addresses include the unspecified address (all zeros), the loopback address (0000:0000:0000:0001) and Anyone addresses, which are a prefix followed by zeros. A packet sent to an Anyone address goes to the nearest system that has that prefix, which is usually used with source routing to steer a packet through chosen transit domains.
sections.eli5: An address is like a phone number where the first digits mean the area and the last digits mean the exact phone. A multicast address is like a group chat name, and an Anyone address means "whoever in this area is closest".

sections.title: Packet Size, Source Routing and Fragmentation
sections.content:
SIP requires every link to have an MTU of 576 octets or more, with link-specific fragmentation underneath if a link cannot carry that. Systems are expected to implement Path MTU Discovery, but a minimal implementation, for example in a boot ROM, may just send packets of 576 octets or less. Unlike IPv4, no Don't Fragment flag is needed, because every SIP packet implicitly has that property.

The Source Routing header carries a list of addresses, a Num Addrs count and a Next Addr index. It is processed only when it reaches the system named in the Destination Address. That system swaps the Destination Address with the next listed address and forwards the packet, until Next Addr equals Num Addrs and the payload is delivered locally.

The Fragmentation header is not for general fragmentation: routers must not fragment packets that are too big, and instead send an ICMP Packet Too Big message. It exists for tunnels and for translated IPv4 fragments. Its Identification field is 32 bits, and every SIP system must be able to reassemble a packet of up to 1024 octets.
sections.eli5: Routers will not cut a too-big parcel into pieces. They send it back and say "make it smaller". Only in a few special cases does the sender cut the parcel up on purpose.

sections.title: Changes to ICMP, IGMP and Transports
sections.content:
Moving from IPv4 to SIP means changing the protocols around it. ICMP is used with Payload Type 1 and IGMP with Payload Type 2. Both now include a pseudo-header in their checksum, like TCP and UDP. ICMP error messages carry the first 256 octets of the invoking packet instead of the IPv4 header plus 64 bits.

Some ICMP codes get new names, such as code 4 becoming packet too big, whose minimum Next-Hop MTU value is 576. Several types are not used: Source Quench, Timestamp, Information Request and Address Mask messages among them.

Transports must use 64-bit addresses. Three service differences matter: SIP does not enforce a maximum packet lifetime, it does not checksum its own header, so the UDP checksum becomes mandatory, and it does not normally fragment, so transports must not send more than 576 octets unless they do Path MTU Discovery. On links where IPv4 uses ARP, the same ARP protocol is used with the low-order 32 bits of the SIP address.
sections.eli5: If you change the shape of the envelope, the post office, the sorting machines and the mailbox labels all need small changes too. This section lists them.

sections.title: An Unfinished Record
sections.content:
The original Internet-Draft by Steve Deering was posted on November 10, 1992. RFC 8507 publishes it substantially unchanged, edited by Bob Hinden, as part of the record of the IETF's IPng work. The document says plainly that it is not complete and is not intended to be implementable.

The gaps are visible. The Security Considerations section says only that it is to be done, and the design rationale in Appendix A is marked as still to be done. Some values, such as the Payload Types for the Source Routing and Fragmentation headers, are left as TBD. Appendix B lists possible future directions, among them carrying full 64-bit addresses in ARP, defining the 28-bit Reserved field as a Flow ID, and adding authentication and integrity mechanisms.

SIP evolved into SIP Plus (RFC 1710), which was assessed as an IPng candidate in RFC 1752 and led eventually to IPv6, first published as RFC 1883.
sections.eli5: This is an old draft of a plan, with some pages still blank. It is kept in the history book because it was one step on the way to the internet addresses we use now.

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: IP version number, decimal 6 (to be confirmed).

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Zero on transmission; ignored on reception.

fields.name: Payload Type
fields.desc: Identifies the type of payload, e.g., TCP.

fields.name: Hop Limit
fields.desc: Decremented by 1 at each forwarding system; packet discarded at zero.

fields.name: flgs
fields.desc: Three reserved zero flags and the T flag (0 permanent, 1 transient).

fields.name: scop
fields.desc: Scope value, from intra-system (1) to global (E).

fields.name: group ID
fields.desc: Identifies the multicast group within the scope.
